transcript.text: Good morning, everyone. We have four weeks before our response is due on the shareholder derivative complaint, and no response has been authorized yet. I'd like to use our weekly litigation and governance review to get a full picture before we move forward. I'll need current reports from litigation, governance, insurance, and board-relations counsel so we can make an informed decision on how to respond. Let's start by hearing where things stand on each front.

transcript.text: Good morning, Elena. On the litigation front, I've completed my initial review of the complaint and the controlling state precedent. I have a significant finding regarding demand futility that I need to share with the group — specifically, my analysis shows that five of the seven directors were independent at the time the demand was made, which has direct implications for the demand-futility allegations. I've prepared an internal memorandum on this point but haven't circulated it yet. I'd like to walk through that analysis now so it can inform our decision on how to respond.

transcript.text: Good morning, Elena and Thomas. Before we get too far into the litigation strategy, I need to flag something important on the governance side. My review of the company's bylaws has uncovered a procedural requirement that will directly affect how we structure any board-level response to this complaint. I'd like to share that with the group now so it's factored into our planning from the outset, rather than discovered later when we're already deep into crafting our response.

transcript.text: Good morning, Elena. On the insurance coverage front, I need to flag a critical timing issue before we proceed. I've reviewed the applicable D&O policy, and it requires that the carrier receive notice within exactly 10 business days of any claim or circumstance that could give rise to a claim. Additionally, the carrier must give written consent before the company makes any admission or enters any settlement. The policy review is currently in my coverage file pending this weekly review, but given the 10-business-day notice deadline, we need to act on this immediately or we risk losing coverage for this matter.

transcript.text: Good morning, Elena. On the board-relations front, I need to share an important constraint that will affect any settlement discussions. The board chair has told me that if the company pursues a negotiated resolution, the board will authorize governance reforms only — no monetary payment and no admission of wrongdoing. I recorded this instruction in my board-relations notes, but it has not yet been placed in the litigation plan. This is critical for everyone to know now, especially given Victor's point about the carrier's consent requirement for any admission or settlement, and Thomas's demand-futility analysis which may shape whether we even pursue a negotiated path.

Second, Thomas, please walk us through your demand-futility analysis now, because the independence of five of seven directors will directly shape whether we pursue a motion to dismiss or a negotiated resolution. Let's proceed in this order: Victor on the notice timeline, Thomas on demand futility, Nadia on the bylaw requirement, and Maya on the scope of the chair's instruction.

transcript.text: Elena, my review of the company's bylaws has uncovered a critical procedural requirement that will affect any board-level response to this complaint. The bylaws provide that any resolution containing a governance undertaking — which would include any governance reforms of the kind Maya mentioned the chair is contemplating — must be approved by a special committee of exactly three independent directors. This requirement applies even if the court has not yet ruled on the complaint. I should note that I have confirmed this requirement but have not yet updated the board-resolution checklist to reflect it. Given that we may be pursuing governance reforms as part of a negotiated resolution, and given Thomas's finding that five of seven directors are independent, we need to factor this special-committee requirement into our planning from the outset. We'll need to identify which three independent directors would serve on that special committee and ensure the proper procedural approvals are in place before any governance-undertaking resolution is brought forward.

That consent requirement is separate from the 10-business-day notice deadline, which I'm addressing now. I'll report back once the notice has been transmitted and will flag any carrier response or conditions they attach.

transcript.text: Elena, to answer your question about the scope of the chair's instruction: the chair framed this specifically around a negotiated resolution — meaning if the company pursues a settlement path, the board will only authorize governance reforms, with no monetary payment and no admission of wrongdoing. The chair did not address the litigation path in that instruction, so I cannot tell you whether the same constraint would apply if we pursue a motion to dismiss or other litigation strategy. That's something I would need to clarify directly with the chair. That said, Nadia's bylaw point is critical here — if governance reforms are going to be part of any resolution, we need a special committee of three independent directors convened, and Thomas has identified five independent directors who could serve. I'd recommend I go back to the chair to confirm the scope of the instruction and flag the special-committee requirement, so the board understands the procedural steps that any governance-reform resolution will require. I'll also formally enter the chair's instruction into the litigation plan so it's documented for the full team.
